content: PAK5, a serine/threonine-protein kinase, is an enzyme encoded by the PAK5 gene in humans. It belongs to the Group II PAK family of serine/threonine kinases and is evolutionarily conserved across species. PAK5 was initially identified as a brain-specific kinase, predominantly expressed in the brain, and is thought to play a role in promoting neurite growth in neuronal cells. Its signaling selectivity is evident in its ability to activate the JNK kinase pathway while not affecting p38 or ERK kinases. The PAK5 gene is the longest among the PAK family and contains 12 exons, with four exons dedicated to the 5’-UTR and the remaining eight coding for the protein. Alternative splicing of the PAK5 gene produces three transcripts, one of which encodes a protein consisting of 719 amino acids. Another transcript is a non-coding RNA that retains introns. Structurally, PAK5 shares similarities with PAK4 and contains a kinase domain and a CDC42/Rac1 interactive binding (CRIB) motif. The protein encoded by PAK5 is a member of the PAK family of Ser/Thr protein kinases, which are known effectors of Rac and CDC42 GTPases. These GTPases are involved in regulating cytoskeletal dynamics, cell proliferation, and survival signaling. PAK5 binds to CDC42 in the presence of GTP and is predominantly expressed in the brain. It promotes neurite outgrowth, suggesting a role in neurite development. Additionally, PAK5 associates with microtubule networks and induces microtubule stabilization. Its subcellular localization is tightly regulated during cell cycle progression. Alternative splicing of PAK5 transcripts results in variants encoding the same protein. Genetic deletion of PAK5, with or without PAK6 deletion, in mice has been linked to defects in locomotion, memory, and learning. PAK5 is co-expressed with DISC1, a gene associated with psychosis risk, and this pathway may modulate synapse plasticity. Physiological levels of PAK5 are associated with overall physical activity in mice, as PAK5 deletion leads to increased activity upon amphetamine stimulation. PAK5 is also thought to be a genetic variant regulating gene expression (eQTL), and its expression is associated with inhibited glucose-regulated insulin secretion in INS1 cells. PAK5 expression is positively regulated by Aurora-A, and both PAK5 and Aurora-A are co-upregulated in esophageal squamous carcinoma. PAK5 levels are also regulated by miR-129 in hepatocellular carcinoma cells and by the binding of the long non-coding RNA CRNDE to miR-186 in glioma cells. PAK5 phosphorylates Pacsin-1 and Synaptojanin-1, thereby regulating synaptic vesicle trafficking. It also phosphorylates GATA1 at S161 and S187, contributing to epithelial-mesenchymal transition. Phosphorylation of p120-catenin at S288 by PAK5 plays a role in cytoskeleton remodeling. In addition to its cytoplasmic localization, PAK5 is also found in mitochondria, where it phosphorylates BAD at S112. PAK5 inhibits MARK2/Par1 activity and modulates microtubule dynamics. Clinically, PAK5 levels are upregulated in various cancers, including osteosarcoma, hepatocellular carcinoma, gastric cancer, glioma, esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, colon cancer, ovarian cancer, and breast cancer. Activating gain-of-function mutations in PAK5 have been observed in non-small-cell lung cancer. PAK5 promotes cancer cell survival and enhances their sensitivity to chemotherapy.
